title: Gregory of Narek (27 February)
hookLine: an Armenian monk whose Book of Lamentations is a conversation with God from the depths

cards: In some Armenian homes there's a book kept near the bed, or tucked under the pillow of someone who is sick. It's a book of prayers, and people often call it simply by its author's village: the Narek.
Tradition says families read from it at bedsides and in hard nights, the way others keep a rosary in a pocket. Its author was a monk at a monastery called Narek, by a lake in Armenia, long ago.
His book starts from the bottom.

teach.h: SPEAKING WITH GOD FROM THE DEPTHS.
teach.b: Gregory called his book a Book of Lamentations. Each of its prayers, by tradition, opens with the same phrase, which can be put in English as speaking with God from the depths of the heart.
Gregory doesn't write as a holy man explaining prayer to beginners. He writes as someone who has looked honestly at himself and doesn't like all he sees.
He piles up images for his own brokenness: a ship breaking apart, a field gone to weeds, a debtor with nothing to pay. Page after page, he refuses to pretend.
And then, again and again, he turns: not to his own goodness, which he's just given up on, but to God's mercy, which he trusts more than his own despair.
He even prays for the people who will read him, and for those who wrong him. That shape is old; the Psalms have it.

In the Douay-Rheims, the psalm Catholics know as the De profundis begins: "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." Gregory's book reads like that first line, carried across page after page.
He belongs first to the Armenian Apostolic Church, which honors him as a saint.

teach.h: AN ARMENIAN DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.
teach.b: Armenian Catholics honor him too, and Pope Francis named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Catholic Church. A monk who wrote so honestly about how lost he was became a teacher.

teach.h: OUT OF THE DEPTHS I HAVE CRIED TO THEE.
teach.b: Prayer doesn't have to start from the top.

how: Armenian Christians, both Apostolic and Catholic, honor Saint Gregory of Narek, and some families keep his Book of Lamentations at home for prayer, especially in illness; in the Roman calendar he is remembered on 27 February.

games.q: you're a monk sitting down to write prayers. you've looked honestly at yourself and you don't like all you see. how do you begin?
o: write only praise, and leave yourself out.
wait until you've become better before writing.
start from the depths, honestly, and turn to mercy.
games.why: Gregory's prayers open by speaking with God from the depths of the heart: honest about himself, and trusting mercy more than his despair.

practice: Let one honest thing rise, something you're carrying that isn't tidy, a failure, a fear, a grudge, a tiredness, and don't dress it up or argue it down.
Then turn, the way Gregory does: if you pray, say the psalm's first line, out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord, and leave the rest to God.
If you don't, breathe out slowly and let the heavy thing sit beside you rather than on top of you.

wordCard.voice: De profundis, Latin for out of the depths, the psalm Gregory of Narek's prayers echo. An Armenian monk, he speaks with God from the depths of the heart, and is a Doctor of the Church.
